newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan banks heading to profit after write-off pain.
newsitem.headline: Japan banks heading to profit after write-off pain.

text.p: Japan's big banks are likely to bounce back into profit with their interim results and write off another chunk of problem loans, thanks to stable stock prices and low interest rates, analysts and bank officials say.

The banks' balance sheets for the six months to September 30 are unlikely to hold any big surprises for financial markets, with earnings and write-offs likely to match the institutions' own forecasts issued in May, they said.
"There were no factors which disturbed their earnings forecasts," said Yushiro Ikuyo, first vice president of Smith Barney International Inc.

Earlier this year, the banks surprised the markets when they announced bigger than expected losses for the full fiscal year to March 1996 due to extensive write-offs of problem loans, many of them dating from the 1980s "bubble era".

With a lot of the pain now behind them, the half-year results in November should show a return to the black, with the five biggest banks expecting to post around the same combined profit that they made in the first half of fiscal 1995/96.

An official at the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd (IBJ) said its half-year result would probably be in line with its forecast. IBJ set a target of disposing of about 100 billion yen ($892 million) of problem loans for 1996/97 and the bank is growing confident of achieving this, he also said.

Last fiscal year, 17 of the nation's 21 biggest banks dripped red ink on a parent current earnings basis despite record operating profits -- profits from banking business before loan loss provisions. The 21 banks disposed of a combined 10.7 trillion yen ($95.5 billion) of problem loans in 1995/96, including loans to failed housing loan firms.

The nation's top five banks -- Sakura, Fuji, Sumitomo, Sanwa and Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi -- estimate their combined parent current profit for the first half of 1996/97 at 247 billion yen ($2.20 billion), slightly down from the 254.45 billion yen ($2.27 billion) a year earlier.

Analysts expect the nation's big banks, now 20 after a merger between Mitsubishi and Bank of Tokyo in April, to dispose of 3.5 trillion yen ($31.2 billion) to 4.0 trillion yen ($35.7 billion) of problem loans in 1996/97.

Among the 17 banks in the red in the last fiscal year, Fuji Bank Ltd's parent current loss was the largest at 500.09 billion yen ($4.46 billion). Fuji Bank president Yoshiro Yamamoto told Reuters last month that the bank has brought problem loans down to a manageable level and will be able to cover the rest with operating profits.

For the full 1996/97 year, analysts expect combined operating profits at the 20 banks to be some four trillion yen ($35.7 billion). Of the total, seven major trust banks are expected to have a combined 1.3 trillion yen ($11.6 billion) operating profits against 654 billion yen ($5.83 billion).
Japan eased special reserve requirements for trust banks in March, freeing up funds to dispose of problem loans.

Even taking this into account, full-year operating profits at the 20 banks will not exceed last fiscal year's record of 4.77 trillion yen ($42.5 billion) because bank lending continued to slow down due to weak economic recovery.

Expectations that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) may tighten its easy monetary policy have made banks cautious about actively engaging in bond trading and interest rate swaps, which were highly profitable for the banks last fiscal year.

However, the 20 banks expect combined parent current profit of 1.23 trillion yen ($10.9 billion) for 1996/97. Current earnings include gains or losses on stock sales. Analysts expect the banks to sell stocks to help post current profits. ($1=112 yen)
